lessons.title: Base weight and the big three
lessons.objective: You can define base weight and name the big three.

payload.prompt: About how many pounds does 3 liters of water weigh?

explanation.correct: A liter of water weighs about 2.2 pounds, so 3 liters is roughly 6.6 pounds. That is exactly why base weight leaves water out: it changes all day and would hide the gear you actually chose.
explanation.incorrect: One liter of water weighs about 2.2 pounds, so 3 liters is close to 6.6. Water is heavy enough to swamp a base weight number, which is why gear nerds count it separately.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Water is over two pounds a liter, so I count it separately."

payload.prompt: Match each pack-weight word to what it means:

pairs.definition: Your pack contents without food, water and fuel
The three heaviest items: pack, shelter and sleep system
Food, water and fuel that get used up along the way
Everything on your body and in your pack, added together

explanation.summary: Base weight ignores consumables so the number stays comparable from trip to trip. Skin-out weight is the honest total, and the big three are where most of the savings usually hide.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Is that base weight or skin-out? Big difference."

payload.prompt: Which trio makes up the big three?

options.text: Pack, shelter and sleep system
options.explanation: These are usually the heaviest and most expensive items, so they are the first place gear nerds look for savings.

options.text: Food, water and fuel
options.explanation: Those are consumables, the exact things base weight leaves out.

options.text: Boots, trekking poles and stove
options.explanation: Useful gear, but not the three heaviest categories in most packs.

options.text: Phone, map and compass
options.explanation: That is a navigation kit, and a light one. It is not what people mean by the big three.

explanation.correct: The big three are your pack, your shelter and your sleep system (bag or quilt plus pad). They tend to be the heaviest gear you carry, so a swap here saves more than trimming small items.
explanation.incorrect: The big three are pack, shelter and sleep system. They are usually the heaviest items, so changing one often saves more weight than cutting ten small things.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Which of the big three did you swap first?"

payload.prompt: Her base weight is 12 lb. Does that include today's water?

scene.alt: A hiker's pack on a hanging scale at a trailhead with a full water bottle sitting beside it on the ground.

explanation.correct: Base weight leaves out consumables: food, water and fuel. Her real load on the trail will be heavier, especially on a long dry stretch where she carries extra water.
explanation.incorrect: By convention, base weight is the pack without food, water and fuel. Water is a consumable, so her true carried weight is higher than 12 pounds.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Twelve pounds base, so what's it with food and water?"

payload.prompt: Finish the definition the way gear nerds say it:
payload.template: Base weight leaves out {{out}}. The big three are your pack, your shelter and your {{third}}.

explanation.correct: Base weight is everything except consumables, so safety gear like a first-aid kit and rain jacket stay in the count. The third of the big three is your sleep system.
explanation.incorrect: Base weight leaves out only food, water and fuel, never safety items like first aid or a rain layer. The big three are pack, shelter and sleep system.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Base weight skips consumables, not safety gear."

lessons.title: Ultralight trade-offs
lessons.objective: You can explain what ultralight gains and gives up.

payload.prompt: What is the fair way to describe the ultralight trade-off?

options.text: Less weight and easier miles, in exchange for less comfort, durability and margin
options.explanation: Both sides are real: lighter gear is often more delicate, less roomy and less forgiving when conditions turn.

options.text: Lighter is always better, with no downside
options.explanation: Every ounce cut usually costs something in comfort, durability, cost or skill.

options.text: Ultralight is a fad that never actually helps anyone
options.explanation: Many hikers find lighter packs mean less fatigue and fewer aches. The approach works for a lot of people.

options.text: It only matters on thru-hikes of thousands of miles
options.explanation: A lighter pack can make a day or weekend hike more comfortable too.

explanation.correct: Ultralight is a real trade. You gain comfort while moving and often more miles. You give up some comfort in camp, some durability and some margin, so it asks for more skill and attention.
explanation.incorrect: Neither "always better" nor "pointless" is fair. Lighter gear helps many hikers, and it also costs something: durability, comfort, money or safety margin if you cut the wrong thing.
explanation.sayThisLine: "What did you give up to get it that light?"

statement.speaker: She
statement.text: I'm ultralight, so no camp chair, no extra clothes, and I sleep under a quilt. But I always keep my rain jacket and first-aid kit.

payload.question: What is she telling you?

options.text: She carries very little on purpose, but keeps her safety basics
options.explanation: Yes. Ultralight means cutting comfort items and duplicates, not the gear that protects you.

options.text: She cannot afford normal gear
options.explanation: Nothing she said is about money. Ultralight is a choice, and light gear often costs more.

options.text: She skips safety gear to save weight
options.explanation: She named her rain jacket and first-aid kit as things she never cuts.

options.text: She is new and does not know what to pack
options.explanation: Her list sounds deliberate. She has decided what to leave behind and what to keep.

payload.translation: She cuts comfort items to keep her pack very light, but treats rain protection and first aid as non-negotiable.
payload.noFakeExpertNote: Ask what she would never leave behind. Curiosity works better than pretending you have opinions about quilts.

followUps.line: What's the one thing you'd never cut, even to save weight?
followUps.why: It invites her to share her rules and shows you understand cutting has limits.

followUps.line: Do you miss the camp chair at the end of a long day?
followUps.why: It is a friendly, honest question about the comfort trade-off she chose.

payload.prompt: You are trimming pack weight the night before a mountain day hike. What do you cut?

situation.narrative: Your pack weighs more than you like. On the bed: a rain jacket, an insulating layer, a first-aid kit, a headlamp, a camp chair and a second water bottle. The forecast is mostly clear with some afternoon cloud.

options.label: Leave the chair and extra bottle; keep jacket, layer, first aid, headlamp
options.consequence: You drop weight from things that only add comfort, and you keep the gear that protects you if weather, injury or darkness surprise you.
considerations: Cut comfort and duplicates first, safety items last.
Mountain weather changes faster than forecasts.

options.label: Weigh it all, then test the lighter setup on a short local hike
options.consequence: A shakedown catches mistakes cheaply near home. It works best if you still count the safety items as fixed.
considerations: Test changes before a big trip, not during one.
Note what you truly used, but remember safety items are for the day things go wrong.

options.label: Leave the rain jacket and insulating layer since the forecast is mostly clear
options.consequence: Wet and wind together can chill you fast, and a forecast is not a promise. Saving a pound is not worth being underdressed high up.
considerations: Forecasts miss, especially in the mountains.
Insulation and rain protection are core safety gear, not extras.

options.label: Leave the first-aid kit and headlamp since you plan to be back before dark
options.consequence: Delays and injuries are exactly when plans slip. A small kit and a light weigh very little compared with what they can do for you.
considerations: Plans slip most when you need the gear.
These are among the lightest, most valuable items you carry.

payload.expertNote: Careful ultralight hikers cut duplicates and comfort items and keep the Ten Essentials as systems. A very low weight is a goal, not a reason to skip protection.
payload.sayThisLine: "I'll leave the chair, not the rain jacket."
payload.safetyNote: Never cut the Ten Essentials to save weight. Follow official guidance and match your kit to the conditions, terrain and your skill.

payload.prompt: Put a shakedown hike in order:

items.text: Lay out and weigh your gear at home
items.why: You cannot improve a number you have not measured, and laying it out shows duplicates.

items.text: Make one or two changes, not ten
items.why: A few changes at a time lets you tell which one helped or hurt.

items.text: Hike or camp with it near home, close to help
items.why: A cheap test in easy conditions catches problems while a fix is still simple.

items.text: Note what worked, what hurt and what you missed
items.why: Honest notes turn one trip into information for the next.

items.text: Adjust, keeping your safety gear fixed
items.why: Unused does not mean unnecessary. First aid and insulation earn their weight on the bad day.

explanation.correct: Weigh it, change a little, test close to home, review honestly, then adjust while keeping safety gear fixed. The order keeps changes cheap and safe.
explanation.incorrect: Measure first, change little, test near help, review, then adjust. Keep safety gear fixed even if you never used it, because it is there for the day things go wrong.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Test it near home before you bet a big trip on it."

payload.prompt: You never touched your first-aid kit on the shakedown. Leave it home?

scene.alt: A small first-aid kit sitting unopened on a picnic table beside a laid-out array of camping gear.

explanation.correct: Safety gear is meant to sit unused. Not needing it on an easy test hike says nothing about the day you do. Trim other items and keep the kit.
explanation.incorrect: Unused is not the same as unnecessary. First aid, insulation and light are for the unplanned day, so a smooth shakedown does not prove they are dead weight.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Safety gear earns its place by staying in the pack."

lessons.title: Trail runners or boots
lessons.objective: You can present both sides of the shoe debate.

payload.prompt: Which statement gives trail runners fair credit AND names a real trade-off?

options.text: They are light and dry fast, but wear out sooner and give less sole protection than boots
options.explanation: Fair to both sides: the fans have real reasons and the critics have real points.

options.text: They are better than boots for every hiker on every trail
options.explanation: "Every" is the giveaway. Heavy loads, snow and rough ground can change the answer.

options.text: Boots are the only responsible choice and runners are reckless
options.explanation: Millions of hikers use trail runners sensibly. Calling them reckless is unfair.

options.text: There is no real difference between the two
options.explanation: There are differences in weight, drying time, durability, protection and warmth.

explanation.correct: Trail runners are lighter, more breathable and need little break-in. Boots often last longer and add sole and ankle protection, plus warmth. Each fits some hikers and some conditions better.
explanation.incorrect: Both sides have points. Runners win on weight, breathability and quick drying. Boots often win on durability, protection and cold or heavy-load conditions. Absolute claims either way miss that.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Runners are light and dry fast, boots are tougher. Depends on the trip."

statement.speaker: Maya
statement.text: I'm a trail-runner convert. Boots feel like ankle prisons. Blisters are down, but my ankles do get tired on rocky ground.

payload.question: What is Maya really saying?

options.text: She prefers light trail shoes and has noticed both benefits and a cost
options.explanation: Yes. She likes the freedom and fewer blisters, and she is honest that rough ground tires her ankles.

options.text: She thinks everyone should give up boots
options.explanation: That is her personal experience, not a rule for anyone else.

options.text: She has a serious ankle injury
options.explanation: She only said her ankles get tired on rocky ground. That is not an injury.

options.text: She only runs and never hikes
options.explanation: Trail runners are just the shoe. She is talking about hiking in them.

payload.translation: She switched to lightweight trail shoes, likes the comfort and fewer blisters, and honestly notes that rocky terrain works her ankles harder.
payload.noFakeExpertNote: You do not need a shoe opinion. Ask what changed for her feet, and let her tell the story.

followUps.line: What made you switch from boots?
followUps.why: Open and curious. It lets her explain her own experience.

followUps.line: How do you handle wet feet in the morning?
followUps.why: Touches the wet-foot trade-off without needing you to have a view.

payload.prompt: A cold, wet spring trip is coming. Which shoe plan is sensible?

situation.narrative: You and a friend plan a two-day trip in the mountains. Highs will be near 40 F with rain likely and old snow patches on the trail. Your friend loves trail runners. You have only ever worn boots.

options.label: Pick footwear for cold, wet conditions and bring spare dry socks
options.consequence: You treat the debate as a tool choice. In cold and wet, keeping feet warm and having dry socks for camp matters more than any philosophy.
considerations: Wet feet plus cold air is a warmth problem, not just a comfort one.
Whatever you wear, pack spare dry socks for camp.

options.label: Wear trail runners with warm socks and change into dry socks at camp
options.consequence: Works for many experienced hikers who are comfortable with wet feet, if they stay moving, keep warm and have a dry pair for camp.
considerations: Be honest about your own experience in cold and wet.
Turn back or add layers if your feet get cold and numb.

options.label: Wet feet are just part of it, so ignore cold or numb toes and keep walking
options.consequence: Cold, numb feet are a warning sign. Ignoring them can lead to cold injury and makes it harder to think and move safely.
considerations: Wet-foot philosophy is about comfort and blisters, not ignoring cold.
Stop, warm up and dry off if your feet go numb.

options.label: Copy your friend's shoes just because she swears by them
options.consequence: Her setup matches her feet, experience and habits, not yours. A new shoe on a cold, wet trip is a bad experiment.
considerations: Fit and familiarity matter more than the trend.
Break in any new footwear before a real trip.

payload.expertNote: Experienced hikers use both, depending on conditions. Runners are popular in warm, dry, well-maintained trails. In cold, wet or snowy conditions, many prefer more protective footwear or extra layers for their feet.
payload.sayThisLine: "Runners are great in summer. For a cold, wet trip I'd want to think it through."
payload.safetyNote: Cold, wet feet can lead to cold injury. Follow official guidance, check the forecast and turn back if your feet go numb.

payload.prompt: A warm afternoon, shallow creek crossing. Wet-foot philosophy says?

scene.alt: A hiker in trail shoes splashing straight through a shallow, slow creek on a warm sunny day while another hiker balances on stones.

explanation.correct: In warm weather, shallow, safe crossings are where wet-foot philosophy shines: shoes drain and dry while you walk. Only cross where the water is slow and clearly safe.
explanation.incorrect: Wet-foot philosophy accepts wet shoes when it is warm. A long detour or a risky rock hop often costs more than a quick, safe splash through a shallow crossing.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Shallow and warm? We'll just walk through."

payload.ruleTag: Wet feet are fine when warm and safe

payload.prompt: Match each shoe-debate idea to what it means:

pairs.definition: Let shoes get wet and drain instead of fighting to stay dry
Wearing new footwear before a big trip so it fits your feet
Stiffness that shields feet from sharp rock on rough ground
How quickly a shoe sheds water after it gets wet

explanation.summary: Wet-foot philosophy is a choice about drainage. Break-in and sole protection are where the runners-versus-boots debate gets practical, because fit and rough ground matter more than fashion.
explanation.sayThisLine: "How well do those drain, and how did you break them in?"

lessons.title: Filters compared
lessons.objective: You can compare filter types by speed, weight and failure modes.

payload.prompt: Match each water treatment option to its main trade-off:

pairs.definition: Light and simple, but can be damaged if it freezes
Hang a bag and let it drip; convenient for groups and camp
Heavier and slower, but many can be cleaned in the field
Uses light against germs, but needs clear water and batteries
Very light backup, but needs a wait time and can taste

explanation.summary: Every option trades speed, weight and a way to fail. Squeeze filters can be ruined by freezing, UV needs batteries and clear water, pumps clog less easily but weigh more, and chemicals need patience.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Everything fails somehow. What's your backup?"

payload.prompt: Your squeeze filter sat outside all night below freezing. Now what?

situation.narrative: It is a cold camp morning and your bottle of filtered water has a crust of ice. Your hollow-fiber squeeze filter was left in the vestibule overnight, and it may have frozen with water inside. The next water source is a creek 3 miles away.

options.label: Treat creek water with your backup method, following its instructions
options.consequence: A frozen filter can have hidden damage you cannot see, so you do not trust it. Your backup gets clean water and you avoid a bad guess.
considerations: Damage from freezing may be invisible.
Carrying a backup is why backups exist.

options.label: Boil water at the creek if you have a stove and fuel
options.consequence: Boiling works when you have the fuel and time. It is slower and uses fuel, but it does not depend on a filter that may be damaged.
considerations: Follow current guidance on boiling time, longer at high elevation.
Let hot water cool before you drink or pour it.

options.label: Use the filter anyway; it looks fine and water flows through
options.consequence: Flow does not prove the filter still works. Frozen hollow fibers can crack and let germs through with no sign at all.
considerations: Water flowing is not proof that it filters.
Follow the maker's guidance: a possibly frozen filter is not trustworthy.

options.label: Drink straight from the creek since the water looks clear
options.consequence: Clear water can still carry germs that cause a miserable illness. Looks tell you nothing about safety.
considerations: Treat backcountry water even when it looks clean.
Illness on trail is a bigger problem than the weight of a backup.

payload.expertNote: Many hikers sleep with their filter in a sleeping bag or pocket in freezing weather and carry a lightweight backup. Always check your own filter's instructions.
payload.sayThisLine: "My filter might have frozen, so I'm using the backup."
payload.safetyNote: Follow the manufacturer's instructions and park guidance. If you suspect a filter froze, do not rely on it; use another treatment method.

payload.prompt: A hiker asks if her squeeze filter handles everything. What is the honest answer?

options.text: Most hollow-fiber filters catch bacteria and protozoa but not viruses; check the specs for your area
options.explanation: That is the fair, checkable answer. Some places or situations call for virus treatment.

options.text: Yes, any filter removes every germ and chemical
options.explanation: No filter does everything. Filters differ, and none remove every possible hazard.

options.text: No, filters do nothing and only boiling works
options.explanation: Filters do reduce bacteria and protozoa well. Boiling also works but is not the only option.

options.text: It only improves taste, not safety
options.explanation: Taste is a side effect. Filters exist to remove harmful microbes.

explanation.correct: Most hollow-fiber filters remove bacteria and protozoa such as Giardia, but many do not remove viruses. Check your filter's specs and local guidance, and add a purifier or chemical treatment if viruses are a concern.
explanation.incorrect: No filter does everything. Read your own filter's specs, know what it removes, and follow park guidance on whether you also need to treat for viruses.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Does yours cover viruses, or just bacteria and protozoa?"

payload.prompt: Finish the filter care sentences:
payload.template: Keep a squeeze filter from {{freezing}}, and treat a possibly frozen one as {{status}}.

explanation.correct: Ice can crack the tiny fibers in a hollow-fiber filter, and you cannot see the damage. That is why a possibly frozen filter should be treated as unreliable.
explanation.incorrect: Freezing is the big enemy of a squeeze filter, because it can crack the fibers invisibly. A possibly frozen filter is unreliable, so switch to another treatment method.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Keep it warm at night, or don't trust it."

payload.prompt: Silty, cloudy water. UV purifier alone, or strain it first?

scene.alt: A hiker holding a bottle of cloudy, silty water beside a muddy stream and a small UV purifier pen.

explanation.correct: UV works best in clear water because particles can shade germs from the light. Let silt settle or strain the water through a cloth first, then treat it, or use another method.
explanation.incorrect: Cloudy water blocks UV light from reaching germs. Settle or strain it first, or use a method that handles silt, following your device's instructions.
explanation.sayThisLine: "UV needs clear water, so strain that first."

lessons.title: Paper or phone
lessons.objective: You can explain why many hikers carry both.

payload.prompt: Your phone dies at a junction on a cold afternoon. What do you do?

situation.narrative: You and a friend used your phone map all day. At an unmarked junction, the cold drains your battery and the screen goes dark. There is no signal. You have a paper map and compass in the bottom of your pack.

options.label: Stop, get out the paper map and compass, and confirm the way before walking
options.consequence: This is exactly why many hikers carry both. You stay calm, check your location against landmarks and choose the trail on purpose.
considerations: Stop first, then decide.
A backup only works if you know how to use it.

options.label: Retrace your route to the last spot you were sure of
options.consequence: Going back to the last confirmed point is a sound choice if you are unsure, especially with daylight left. It is slower but keeps you on known ground.
considerations: Leave yourself enough daylight to get out.
Better than guessing at an unmarked junction.

options.label: Pick the path that looks most worn and hope for the best
options.consequence: A worn path may be a social trail or a shortcut. Guessing at a junction is how small mix-ups become being off route.
considerations: Confirm with a map, not a hunch.
Unofficial paths can lead the wrong way.

options.label: Keep trying to restart the phone while daylight burns
options.consequence: You lose time and daylight on a device that may not come back. The map you already carry is the faster fix.
considerations: Use the tool that works now.
Cold batteries often recover briefly when warmed, but do not bet your plan on it.

payload.expertNote: Many hikers use the phone as the everyday tool and treat the paper map and compass as the backup they always carry. What matters is carrying both, downloading offline maps, and practicing with the paper backup before you need it.
payload.sayThisLine: "Phone is my main, and the paper map is the backup."
payload.safetyNote: Carry a paper map and compass and learn to use them. If you are unsure of your location, stop, and stay put if you told someone your plan and cannot retrace confidently.

payload.prompt: Why do many careful hikers carry both a phone and paper?

options.text: Each fails differently: phones lose battery or break, paper cannot show your live position
options.explanation: Two different tools with different weak points make a strong pair.

options.text: Because phones never work outdoors at all
options.explanation: Phone maps with downloaded areas work well without signal. They are not useless.

options.text: Only out of tradition; paper adds nothing
options.explanation: Paper has real strengths: no battery, big-picture view and quick scanning.

options.text: Because the law requires paper maps on every trail
options.explanation: There is no such general rule. It is a personal safety choice.

explanation.correct: Phones give a live blue dot and easy zoom but rely on a battery and can crack or die in the cold. Paper is bulky and static but always on. Carrying both covers each tool's weak point.
explanation.incorrect: Neither tool is perfect. A phone can run out of power or break. A paper map cannot show where you are. Together, one covers the other's failure.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Paper never runs out of battery, phones never get lost in the wind."

payload.prompt: Long day, no signal. Keep the phone searching for service?

scene.alt: A phone on a backpack strap showing a downloaded trail map with no cell bars and the battery indicator steadily dropping.

explanation.correct: A phone hunting for a signal burns battery quickly. Airplane mode with a downloaded offline map keeps your location working and stretches the battery, and you can still switch back if you need to call for help.
explanation.incorrect: Constant searching for service drains the battery. Download the map before you go, use airplane mode on the trail, and save the battery for when you truly need it.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Offline map, airplane mode, and save the battery."

payload.prompt: Put a phone-plus-paper navigation prep in order:

items.text: At home, download the offline map for the whole area
items.why: Signal is unreliable in the backcountry, so the map must already be on the phone.

items.text: Fully charge the phone and pack a small power bank
items.why: The battery is the weak link, especially in cold weather.

items.text: Pack a paper map and compass in a handy spot
items.why: The backup only helps if you can reach it quickly.

items.text: On the trail, use airplane mode and check the map at junctions
items.why: It saves battery and keeps you confirming your route instead of drifting.

items.text: Practice using the paper map before you need it
items.why: A backup you have never used may not work when you are stressed.

explanation.correct: Download the map, charge up, pack the backup, use airplane mode, and practice with paper. Preparing before the trip is what makes the backup usable.
explanation.incorrect: Do the prep at home: offline map, charge, and paper map. Then save battery on trail and practice with the paper map before you ever need it.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Download it, charge it, pack the paper, practice with it."

statement.speaker: She
statement.text: I love my app, but I still bring the paper map. Last winter my phone died in the cold and the map saved us.

payload.question: What is she telling you?

options.text: She uses her phone but carries paper as a backup after a real failure
options.explanation: Yes. She likes the app and keeps the paper map because the phone actually let her down.

options.text: She refuses to use phones outdoors
options.explanation: She said she loves her app. She is not anti-phone.

options.text: She has never had any trouble navigating
options.explanation: She described a phone failure. The map was what got them through.

options.text: She thinks you must never use a phone map
options.explanation: It is her habit, not a rule. She uses both.

payload.translation: She uses a phone app as her main tool, keeps paper as a backup because cold weather killed her battery once, and that backup helped.
payload.noFakeExpertNote: If you have never navigated with a compass, say so and ask how she learned. That reads better than pretending.

followUps.line: How did you learn to use the paper map?
followUps.why: It shows genuine interest in the skill and invites her to share how she learned.

followUps.line: Do you keep the phone in your jacket to save the battery?
followUps.why: It is a friendly follow-up about her cold-weather habits.

lessons.title: Going fast
lessons.objective: You can explain fastpacking and FKTs without mocking either.

statement.speaker: He
statement.text: I'm fastpacking the loop in two days and thinking about logging an FKT attempt. Very light pack, run the flats, hike the climbs.

payload.question: What is he describing?

options.text: Moving fast with a light pack, mixing running and hiking, and chasing a record time
options.explanation: Yes. Fastpacking is fast, light, multi-day travel, and an FKT is a fastest known time on a route.

options.text: Entering an official, timed race
options.explanation: An FKT is an informal, self-reported time, not an organized race.

options.text: Skipping safety gear to save weight
options.explanation: He did not say that. Fast and light does not have to mean careless.

options.text: A casual day hike with friends
options.explanation: Two days, a very light pack and a record attempt are far from a casual stroll.

payload.translation: He plans to cover the route quickly over two days, running the flat sections and hiking climbs with a very light pack, and may try to set a fastest known time.
payload.noFakeExpertNote: You do not need to run trails to be curious. Ask about the planning, not the speed.

followUps.line: How do you plan food and water when you move that fast?
followUps.why: It shows you understand that light packs need careful logistics.

followUps.line: What's your bail-out plan if the weather turns?
followUps.why: A respectful safety question that fast, light travelers take seriously.

payload.prompt: Which take on fastpackers and FKT chasers is fair?

options.text: It takes real fitness and planning, and a lighter kit means a thinner safety margin
options.explanation: Respects the athleticism and honestly names the risk trade-off.

options.text: They are just showing off and ruining the trail
options.explanation: That mocks people without a reason. Most follow the rules like everyone else.

options.text: Anyone can safely copy their pace and gear list
options.explanation: Their fitness, experience and support are part of what makes it work. Copying the kit alone is risky.

options.text: An FKT is an official record certified by the park
options.explanation: FKTs are informal and self-reported, not official park records.

explanation.correct: Fastpacking and FKTs ask for fitness, navigation skill and careful planning. A lighter kit trades away margin, so the people who do it well plan for weather, water and bail-outs.
explanation.incorrect: Skip the mocking and the copying. These athletes bring fitness and experience, and a very light kit thins the safety margin. Both deserve respect and honest caution.
explanation.sayThisLine: "That takes real fitness. How do you plan for bad weather?"

payload.prompt: You want to try fastpacking after hearing her stories. How do you start?

situation.narrative: A friend's fastpacking trip sounded amazing. You are a solid day hiker but have never run with a pack or done a multi-day trip. A mountain loop you like has a storm-prone high section.

facts.label: Idea
facts.value: Match her pace and light kit

options.label: Build up gradually: short light trips, then longer, and set a turnaround time
options.consequence: You gain skills and learn what your body needs before you thin your margin. A pre-set turnaround keeps the storm-prone section honest.
considerations: Add one new challenge at a time.
Being light works best when you also have skills.

options.label: Join her on an easier route and learn how she plans
options.consequence: Learning from an experienced partner on friendlier terrain is a smart, social way in. Keep your own safety gear and speak up if the pace is too much.
considerations: Ask about her planning, not just her kit.
Hike at the pace that is right for you.

options.label: Copy her exact gear list and target her pace on the storm-prone loop
options.consequence: Her kit and pace fit her fitness and experience. Copying them without the skills can leave you underprepared in exposed terrain.
considerations: The gear list is the visible part of a lot of unseen experience.
Storm-prone terrain punishes a thin margin.

options.label: Drop the rain jacket and headlamp to match her light pack
options.consequence: Cutting protection to look light is a weak bargain. If you slow down or the weather turns, you have nothing to fall back on.
considerations: Light does not mean missing the essentials.
Experienced fastpackers still carry core safety items.

payload.expertNote: Fast and light is a skill set built over time. It pairs a light kit with good fitness, navigation, weather judgment and a clear turnaround, so the margin is in the skills instead of the pack.
payload.sayThisLine: "I'd love to try it. Can I start small and learn how you plan?"
payload.safetyNote: Build skills gradually, follow official guidance and check the mountain forecast. Do not copy someone else's kit or pace without their experience.

payload.prompt: Match each go-fast term to its meaning:

pairs.definition: Moving quickly with a light pack, mixing hiking and running
Fastest known time: an informal record for a route
A planned place to leave the route early if things go wrong
Carrying or resupplying your own gear without a crew handing help

explanation.summary: Fastpacking is the style, FKT is the informal goal, and bail-out points are how careful fast movers keep an exit ready. Self-supported means doing it without a crew.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Where are your bail-out points on that route?"

payload.prompt: Complete the fair-minded summary:
payload.template: An FKT is an {{kind}} record. Fast and light travel still needs weather checks and a {{plan}}.

explanation.correct: FKTs are informal and self-reported, kept by the community. Speed does not replace judgment: fast movers still check weather and set a turnaround time before they start.
explanation.incorrect: An FKT is an informal record, not an official one. Fast travelers still need weather checks and a turnaround time, because being quick does not make a storm go away.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Fast or slow, we still set a turnaround time."

lessons.title: Hike your own hike
lessons.objective: You can respect a different style without abandoning safety.

statement.speaker: She
statement.text: Hike your own hike. Some people want heavy comfort and some want to fly. It's all fine unless it puts someone else at risk.

payload.question: What is she saying about styles?

options.text: Respect different styles, but not at the expense of others' safety
options.explanation: Yes. HYOH welcomes different pace, gear and style, and she adds the limit herself.

options.text: Anything goes, safety included
options.explanation: She named a limit: no putting others at risk.

options.text: There is one right way to hike
options.explanation: The opposite of what she said. She welcomes different styles.

options.text: It is only about which gear to buy
options.explanation: She mentioned comfort and speed, which are broader than gear.

payload.translation: She believes in letting people choose their own pace, gear and style, as long as their choices do not endanger anyone else.
payload.noFakeExpertNote: Say what you honestly like, and ask about her style. You do not have to pretend to hike like she does.

followUps.line: What's your style: fast, comfy, or somewhere in the middle?
followUps.why: Invites her to share her approach without ranking anyone's.

followUps.line: Did you ever change your style after a tough trip?
followUps.why: Open and curious. It shows styles can grow and change.

payload.title: Different gear, same trail
payload.setting: Texting after meeting hikers with a very different setup

exchanges.theirMessage: We passed a guy with a huge pack and a camp chair. I carry eight pounds. We just stared at each other.

replies.text: Ha. Different styles. Did he seem happy with his setup?
replies.theirResponse: Honestly, yes. He said the chair is his favorite part of the day.
replies.coachNote: Curious and kind. You treat his choice as valid.
True, but it puts the focus on judging his gear.

replies.text: He should really lighten up. Ultralight is just better.
replies.theirResponse: Hmm, I'd say hike your own hike.

exchanges.theirMessage: I just wish more people knew to stay on the trail. We saw a bunch of shortcuts cutting the switchbacks.

replies.text: Those are social trails, right? They damage the slope. Do rangers mark them?
replies.theirResponse: Sometimes. Cutting switchbacks causes erosion, so it's a real problem.
replies.coachNote: Uses the term correctly and asks a real follow-up.

replies.theirResponse: It is. Small things add up.

replies.text: It's only a few feet. Nobody cares about a shortcut.
replies.theirResponse: It adds up. That's how erosion starts.
replies.coachNote: Shortcuts are exactly how social trails form.

payload.closingNote: Respect for other people's style, and for the trail itself, is the same habit.

payload.prompt: Your friend's style is slower and heavier than yours. Storms are possible. What now?

situation.narrative: You and a friend have different styles: you like to move fast and light, and she brings extra layers, food and a camp comfort kit. She is falling behind and a stretch of open ridge is ahead. Clouds are building, and a social trail offers a steep shortcut.

options.label: Stay at her pace, skip the shortcut, and head down early if clouds keep building
options.consequence: Hike your own hike does not mean leaving someone behind. The group moves at the slowest pace, keeps a clear turnaround, and stays on the marked trail.
considerations: The group hikes at the slowest person's pace.
Marked trails protect the land and keep the route clear.

options.label: Ask her what she wants, then agree on a regroup point and time
options.consequence: Talking it through respects both styles. Set a specific regroup point in sight, and do not lose track of each other in building weather.
considerations: Pick a clear, close regroup place.
Splitting up in a storm setup adds risk.

options.label: Go ahead and wait for her at the summit since your style is faster
options.consequence: You would be alone on exposed ground as storms build, and she would be alone behind you. HYOH does not cover leaving your partner.
considerations: Your style choices should not shift risk onto others.
Stay together when weather is uncertain.

options.label: Cut the steep social trail to save time and catch up
options.consequence: Steep shortcuts erode the slope and can be slippery and unstable. You also add risk of a fall to save a few minutes.
considerations: Social trails damage vegetation and soil.
Staying on the trail is part of Leave No Trace.

payload.expertNote: HYOH is generous about pace, gear and style, and firm about two things: nobody's safety gets traded away for someone else's style, and the trail itself is protected.
payload.sayThisLine: "We'll go at your pace, and we'll set a turnaround so we stay safe."
payload.safetyNote: Groups stay together and move at the slowest member's pace. Follow official guidance, check the forecast, and turn back before storms reach exposed ground.

payload.prompt: What is a social trail, and why does it matter?

options.text: An informal path worn by repeated foot traffic, often a shortcut, that harms plants and soil
options.explanation: Yes. Social trails form when people cut corners, and they cause erosion and damage.

options.text: An official trail built for group hikes
options.explanation: "Social" refers to how it formed, not to groups. These are not official.

options.text: A trail that connects to a hiking club website
options.explanation: Not related to the internet. It is a physical path made by walkers.

options.text: A quiet, scenic side trail that is always safe to follow
options.explanation: Social trails are often steep, unmaintained and unmarked, so they are not always safe.

explanation.correct: A social trail is an unofficial path worn by repeated use, often a switchback shortcut or a route to a viewpoint. It can cause erosion, trample plants and lead you off the planned route.
explanation.incorrect: Social trails are informal paths that people wear into the land, often cutting corners. They harm soil and plants, and they can mislead you. Stay on the marked trail.
explanation.sayThisLine: "That's a social trail. Let's stay on the real one."

payload.prompt: Your friend cuts a switchback: "my hike, my way." Is that HYOH?

scene.alt: A hiker stepping off the main trail to scramble straight down a raw, eroded shortcut between two switchbacks.

explanation.correct: HYOH covers your pace, gear and style, not choices that damage the land or put others at risk. Cutting switchbacks erodes the slope and starts social trails, so it falls outside the motto.
explanation.incorrect: Hike your own hike has limits. Choices that harm the trail or endanger others are not just personal style. Cutting switchbacks causes erosion, so stay on the trail.
explanation.sayThisLine: "HYOH is about pace and gear. Not about wearing down the trail."

payload.ruleTag: HYOH stops at safety and the land
